title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
hookLine: Nathanael scoffs, can anything good come from Nazareth? and is seen before he's met

cards: There's a punchline in this story, and it's a town.
Philip has just met Jesus, and he runs to find his friend Nathanael, bursting with it: we've found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.
And Nathanael answers, in the King James words: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" A hometown, written off in one line. Nathanael, John tells us later, is from Cana.
And Philip doesn't argue. He just borrows Jesus's words from yesterday: come and see.

teach.h: AN ISRAELITE IN WHOM IS NO GUILE.
teach.b: So Nathanael comes, probably still skeptical. Before he can say a word, Jesus sees him coming and says: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!" No guile: nothing fake, no hidden angle.
Nathanael has just insulted Jesus's hometown, and Jesus compliments his honesty. How do you know me?

teach.h: I SAW THEE UNDER THE FIG TREE.
teach.b: And Jesus answers: "Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee." What was Nathanael doing under that fig tree? John doesn't say.
Some readers think of the prophets' picture of peace, everyone sitting under their own vine and fig tree. Some point to later Jewish writings that picture teachers studying under fig trees.
The honest answer is that nobody knows, and that seems to be the point: something private, something only Nathanael would know about, and Jesus saw it.

teach.h: THOU ART THE SON OF GOD.
teach.b: Nathanael's skepticism collapses into a confession: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel." And Jesus, almost amused: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree?
You'll see greater things than these. You'll see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
That's Jacob's ladder from Genesis, the dream where angels go up and down between heaven and earth. Jacob, who took his brother's blessing by deceit, is echoed in a man with no deceit at all.

teach.h: CAN THERE ANY GOOD THING COME OUT OF NAZARETH?
teach.b: And the man who made the Nazareth joke ends up seeing heaven open.

how: Tradition identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew, honored on his feast day, and some lectionaries read the call of Nathanael in the season after Epiphany.

games.q: you're Philip. you tell your friend you've found the one the prophets wrote about, and he sneers: from Nazareth? what do you say?
games.why: Philip doesn't argue. "come and see." and when Nathanael comes, Jesus already knows him.

practice: Think of a place, a group, or a kind of person you've written off with a joke, a town, a school, a profession, a political side, and notice the line you usually say about them.
Imagine a friend taking you there and asking what you're looking for, and picture one good thing you might find. If you pray, you can ask to see people the way Nathanael was seen.

wordCard.voice: Nathanael, whose name means God has given: the skeptic Jesus saw sitting under a fig tree before they ever met, a private moment that turned him into a follower.

orig.note: Hebrew: Nathanael, 'God has given'. in the New Testament, only John's Gospel names him; the same Hebrew name appears in the Old Testament as Nethaneel.

carryVoice: Your line: can anything good come? Philip didn't argue; he invited. Day five hundred ninety-six.
